summary: The reader is built to feel disgust at Gregor and then shame at feeling it, pity for his love and loneliness, and bitter unease at the family's relief.

need-to-breathe.why: Nothing is built to affect the reader's breath.

hungry.why: Gregor's refused food and slow starvation are built to be felt as absence rather than appetite.

full.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

thirsty.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

gassy.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

need-to-poop.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

need-to-pee.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

sleepy.why: The story does not aim to lull.

nauseous.why: The rotting apple in Gregor's back and the fresh milk he spits out are built to turn the reader's stomach a little.

urge-to-sneeze.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

urge-to-cough.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

dizzy.why: Nothing is built to produce vertigo.

fatigued.why: The reader is not made to feel exertion.

pain.why: The apple driven into Gregor's back and left to fester is built to make the reader wince.

disgusted.why: The insect body, the brown fluid, the sticky trail, and the dust-covered dying Gregor are built to disgust the reader, who is then made to feel ashamed of it.

itchy.why: Gregor's itching belly and waving legs are described so the reader's skin crawls a little.

tickled.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

over-stimulated.why: Nothing is built to overwhelm the senses.

too-hot-too-cold.why: Nothing is built to make the reader feel heat or cold.

afraid.why: The chief clerk at the door and the father's apples are built to frighten on Gregor's behalf.

anxious.why: The first morning's mounting pressure, the clock, the knocking, the locked door, is built to make the reader share Gregor's dread.

panic.why: The father's chase with the apples gives the reader a moment of panic for Gregor.

sensory-pleasures.why: Nothing is built to give the reader sensory pleasure.

aesthetic-pleasures.why: The flat, exact prose and the perfect shape of the three sections are built for the reader's pleasure in form.

piquancy.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

orgasm.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

love-romantic.why: The lady in furs is a sad joke; nothing is built to make the reader feel love.

love-family.why: Gregor's tenderness for the family that abandons him is built to make the reader feel the love and its betrayal at once.

grief.why: Gregor's quiet death at dawn is built to make the reader mourn him, since no one in the story does.

missing-someone.why: Gregor listening at the door for his family lets the reader feel his exclusion.

aroused-sexually.why: Nothing is built to arouse the reader.

liking-as-a-friend.why: The reader is built to like Gregor, a dutiful, modest man in a monstrous body.

empathy.why: The narration stays inside Gregor's bewildered, reasonable mind, so the reader feels his every rebuff from within.

compassion.why: Gregor hiding under the sofa so as not to upset his sister, and dying of neglect, are built to produce pity.

grateful.why: Nothing is built to make the reader grateful.

pleasure-from-helping.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

trustful-distrustful.why: The reader watches the family's care turn to betrayal and learns to distrust their every reassurance.

depressed.why: Gregor's bleak decline can lower the reader's mood, which the story intends.

angry.why: The father's apples and Grete's verdict that it must go are built to anger the reader.

envious.why: Nothing is built to produce envy.

jealous-romantic-sexual.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

jealous-friendship.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

hatred.why: The family is built for judgment rather than hatred.

contempt.why: The chief clerk's officiousness, the lodgers' airs, and the charwoman's callousness are built for the reader's scorn.

resentment.why: The family's ingratitude to the son who supported them is built to make the reader feel the injustice.

proud.why: Nothing is built to make the reader proud.

amused.why: Gregor's efforts to get out of bed and the charwoman's cheerful announcement of his death are built as black comedy.

sense-of-belonging.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

lonely.why: Gregor's isolation in his room, visited less and less, is built to make the reader feel loneliness.

judgy-moral-sense.why: The reader is built to judge the family's slide from care to disposal and the ending's tram ride.

admiration.why: Nothing is built to make the reader admire a character.

embarrassed.why: The family's mortification before the chief clerk and the lodgers gives the reader secondhand embarrassment.

shame.why: The reader's own relief at Gregor's death is built to shame the reader, the story's final turn of the screw.

guilt.why: The reader is made faintly complicit in the family's relief.

sad.why: Gregor's decline and death are built to produce sorrow the story's characters refuse.

happy.why: Nothing is built to make the reader content; the family's contentment is the horror.

joyful-euphoric.why: The family's spring tram ride gives a lift the reader is meant to distrust.

effort.why: A short, clear novella; nothing demands persistence.

focused-in-flow.why: The first morning is built to hold the reader rapt from the first sentence.

impatient.why: The reader waits for Gregor to open the door, as the family does.

curious.why: The reader wants to know how the transformation happened and how it will end, questions the story never answers.

surprised.why: The first sentence is built to astonish, and the matter-of-fact tone keeps the astonishment alive.

awe.why: Nothing is built to produce awe.

skeptical-doubtful.why: The flat telling of an impossible event makes the reader distrust the ordinary surface.

feeling-of-knowing.why: Nothing is built to make a clue almost land.

confused.why: The absence of any explanation for the transformation is built to leave the reader unsure how to take it.

frustrated.why: Gregor's inability to make himself understood is built to frustrate the reader who understands him perfectly.

uncertain-certain.why: The reader is kept uncertain whether to read the story as nightmare, parable, or fact.

understanding.why: The story is built so the reader comes to understand it as a parable of use and disposal.

inspired.why: The parable may inspire thought about work and family, which the story leaves to the reader.

satisfied.why: Gregor's death and the family's renewal close the story with a satisfaction the reader is meant to find uneasy.

foreboding.why: The festering apple and the growing neglect are built to make the reader see Gregor's end coming.

nostalgia.why: Gregor's memories of his old life give the reader a faint backward ache.

anticipation-suspense.why: The locked door on the first morning and the lodgers' discovery are built as suspense.

hope.why: The reader hopes Grete will keep caring and Gregor will recover, hopes the story crushes.

schadenfreude.why: Nothing is built to be enjoyed at anyone's expense.

elevation.why: Gregor's dying tenderness lifts the reader faintly.

infatuation.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

rage.why: The father's apples may provoke a flash of rage in the reader.
